Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Newcastle United defender Amar Dedic was reportedly at the centre of a “major police operation” after he was spotted carrying a bow and arrows near a local beauty spot.

The Daily Mail reported that six police cars were called and stopped Dedic’s car northwest of the city in the Darras Hall estate, around seven miles away from where a member of the public had raised the alarm.

Dedic, a £30m signing from Benfica this summer, and a friend were seen carrying a bow and arrows while walking along a countryside reservoir in the Harlow Hill area on Wednesday afternoon.

The bow and arrows were seized by police following questioning, with officers believing the weapon was “for recreational use” and carried no threat to the public. It is unclear what the bow and arrow was used for, however, and enquiries are ongoing.

Decic, a 24-year-old Bosnia and Herzegovina international, remains available to play for Newcastle when they travel to Fulham in the Premier League on Saturday afternoon, following a run of four defeats in five games.

The Daily Mail added that, by sheer coincidence, Newcastle goalkeeper Mark Gillespie and former defender Paul Dummett arrived at the scene while police were speaking to Dedic and offered assistance.

A Northumbria Police spokesperson said: “Shortly after 1.55pm (Wednesday), we received a report of two men carrying a bow and arrows while walking along a track by the reservoir on Military Road in the Harlow Hill area.

“Officers attended and subsequently stopped a vehicle in the Darras Hall area and seized a bow and arrows. At this stage, it is understood they were for recreational use and there was no threat to the public. Enquiries are ongoing.”

Manchester City’s start to the 2026/27 season under Enzo Maresca has received a blow, with reports emerging that Rayan Ait-Nouri’s representatives are actively and publicly seeking a way out of the Etihad Stadium for their client.

The Algerian international, widely regarded as one of Europe’s more dynamic attacking full-backs, has found himself out of the side under the Italian. Frustration has seemingly now reached a point of no return.

According to L'Equipe, which was subsequently relayed by Get French Football News, Ait-Nouri’s camp has lost patience with Maresca’s handling of the 25-year-old.

The player's entourage delivered a blunt assessment of his current predicament, declaring: "He can’t remain in a situation where his talent is wasted."

That admission provides a window into the growing disconnect between Maresca and certain members his squad. Since taking the reins at the Etihad, the former Chelsea boss has adhered to a tactical style that has bypassed Ait-Nouri’s natural overlapping instincts.

Ait-Nouri’s sidelining could be framed as particularly confusing given Man City’s recent struggles to break down low-block defences - a scenario where the Algerian’s ball-carrying ability and final-third delivery usually prove effective.

Instead, he has been restricted to cameo appearances and domestic cup starts, a downgrade in status that has not gone unnoticed by those representing him.

The January transfer window now looks a possible escape route for Ait-Nouri, following his camp's public agitating. With his entourage pushing for a resolution, there will no doubt be a host of Champions League contenders closely monitoring the situation, aware that a player of his calibre rarely becomes available mid-season.

For Maresca, the immediate challenge is finding a way to quell the mounting concerns within his ranks and restore order to the squad.

If players like Ait-Nouri feel their prime years are being squandered, and are emboldened enough to speak out about it, there is every chance more marginalised members of Maresca's squad will follow suit.

City could do with a morale-boosting win after a tough week-and-a-half. Back-to-back Premier League defeats against Aston Villa and Brighton & Hove Albion have seen them lose top spot to Arsenal, while they edged past the Seagulls on penalties in the Carabao Cup fourth round.

Those results served as a reality check after a great start to Enzo Maresca's reign - on the pitch, at least. It has made this trip to Germany more important than it might have looked on paper, especially with matches against Napoli and Barcelona next up in the league phase.

City are well-placed with six points from three games, having seen off Porto and AEK Athens, but more dropped points would harm their chances of finishing in the top eight and qualifying automatically for the last 16.

Maresca should have close to a fully-fit squad available, although he remains without injured winger Antoine Semenyo.

We are backing Maresca's men to return to winning ways, although the German side should pose a stern test.

#1016. When is FA Cup second round draw? Ball numbers, time and how to watch

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The draw for the second round of the FA Cup will take place on Monday 9 November after this weekend’s fixtures

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The FA Cup is in full swing for the 2026-27 season with 40 first round fixtures to be played over the weekend before the draw for the second round takes place on Monday 9 November.

32 non-league sides remain in the competition and will be seeking to stake a claim for a spot in the next round as they come up against the teams from League’s One and Two.

Friday night’s matches see 2021 champions, and former Premier League winners, Leicester City take on the National League’s Oxford City while Bristol Rovers do battle with Cambridge United.

Over the weekend, there are exciting and intriguing fixtures across the board with the potential for the magic of the FA Cup to provide some upsets. League One’s promotion-chasers Bradford City host Marine FC while, AFC Rushden & Diamonds - one of four teams to reach this stage of the competition for the very first time - travel to Burton Albion.

Another of those first-time clubs is Sholing who face fellow non-league side Salisbury in a winnable fixture while the two remaining teams, Plymouth Parkway and Berkhamsted, conclude the first round fixtures on Monday evening and will contest a spot in the next round following the second round draw on TNT Sports.

Other teams of note are former FA Cup winners Sheffield Wednesday (1896, 1907 and 1935) who take on Oldham Athletic, Huddersfield Town (1922) who face Exeter City and Wigan Athletic (2013) who will travel to Boreham Wood.

Here’s everything you need to know about the second-round draw.

The draw for the second round of the 2026-27 FA Cup takes place on Monday 9 November, before the clash between non-league clubs Plymouth Parkway and Berkhamsted.

The television coverage of the game starts at 6:30pm BST, with the draw itself expected to begin shortly afterwards.

The draw will be available to watch live in the UK on TNT Sports 1, HBO Max, and on the TNT Sports YouTube channel. Coverage begins at 6.30pm, with the draw itself expected to start before kick off at 7.30pm.

There will be 40 teams in the draw for the second round with 20 fixtures to be made ahead of the entry of the Premier League and Championship clubs from the third round onwards.

The ball numbers for the draw will be revealed over the weekend closer to the time of the draw itself.

The 20 FA Cup second-round matches will be held across the weekend of 5-6 of December, with the third-round draw presumed to take place on the evening of Monday 7 December.

If these two clubs are doing it, it's worth investigating...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Crossing isn’t exactly a dying art, but it has certainly become rarer to see the more ambitious, attack-minded teams swing crosses into the box from open play.

It just isn’t de rigueur to try something so low-percentage, something so unfashionably anti-aesthetic.

But two of the most attacking clubs (with two of the most modern, zeitgeisty tacticians) pivoted to crossing at the weekend, so it is worth considering whether this is the beginning of a new trend that will catch on.

Fashion, after all, plays an outsized role in tactical theory in the Premier League, and if Brighton and Liverpool are doing it, then it must be Smart and Good.

Liverpool’s 12 open-play crosses in the first half on Sunday were the most any team have managed against Arsenal since November 2020. By the 42nd minute, when Alex Mac Allister should have scored with a header from what was their 19th cross (open or set-piece) of the match, Liverpool had almost quadrupled the five crosses they made in the whole game against Brighton the weekend before.

Brighton weren’t as consistent in their 2-0 victory over Manchester City, but there was a clear tactical plan to switch the play with long diagonals into the (very wide) wingers as often as possible. Fabian Hurzeler appeared to see City’s not-actually-full-backs as the weak spot, and it worked, leading directly to the winning goal.

Liverpool and Brighton had different reasons for their strategies, although the end result was the same: both knew that by getting balls into the box they could sew chaos. Brighton’s winner came via a deflected half-clearance, while Arsenal’s defence regularly made first contact but, now on the back foot, were penned in by the loose second ball (at their most dishevelled, Jurrien Timber pulled on Alexander Isak’s shirt).

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

As Iraola put it: “We’ve put them under pressure, we’ve put them inside the box, we’ve put them there.”

Arsenal, uncomfortable, were pushed back into the box; were 'put there'. It is a simple, albeit unfashionable, idea that others may choose to follow.

Alex Keble is a freelance football journalist based in London, specialising in tactical analysis. He has written for BBC Sport, Goal, The Mirror, The Independent, Football 365, and many others. As well as covering Premier League football, Alex works as a child therapist.

#1013. Anderson in talks with Surrey after Lancashire release

Sky Sports News understands James Anderson is in talks with Surrey to extend his country cricket career; Anderson was released by Lancashire after last season, despite taking 50 wickets and serving as captain

James Anderson is in talks to join Surrey next season and extend his career in county cricket.

Anderson, 44, was released by boyhood club Lancashire in October after over 25 years of service, a decision he said left him "sad" and "quite shocked" and made him question if there was something "fundamentally wrong with me as a person".

England's all-time leading wicket-taker told his BBC podcast Tailenders last month that he had not decided whether to pursue a deal elsewhere, but Sky Sports News understands he is in negotiations with Surrey and could play at The Kia Oval, a venue where he claimed 50 wickets in 16 Tests between 2003 and 2023.

Anderson, who turns 45 in July of next year, could now get the chance to increase his haul of 1,193 first-class wickets and perhaps add more silverware to a glittering CV that includes four Ashes series victories and the 2010 T20 World Cup in the Caribbean.

The Burnley-born bowler picked up 50 wickets at an average of 17.68 in County Championship Division Two for Lancashire in 2026.

His exit from Old Trafford came as the hierarchy, including new director of cricket Paul Farbrace, plot to build an attack for the future after a poor few seasons in red-ball cricket.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Anderson captained Lancashire last term as the county finished second bottom of the second tier, ahead of only Gloucestershire.

The seamer - who is poised to play in the Italia T10 for Napoli Knights later this month - was forced into international retirement by England in 2024.

Anderson took four wickets in his final Test, against West Indies at Lord's, to end with 704 wickets across 188 games in the longest format, at an average of 26.45.

He is the most prolific pace bowler in Test history, with only Sri Lankan off-spinner Muttiah Muralitharan (800) and Australian leg-spinner Shane Warne (708) taking more wickets.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Speaking on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast recently, Michael Atherton disagreed with the views of some that Lancashire had handled Anderson's release badly.

"When somebody like Farbrace comes in as director of cricket at Lancashire, or in England's case Rob Key, when they've decided to move on, how do you do that?" said Sky Sports pundit and former England captain Atherton.

"In both instances, Anderson was told face to face. It wasn't done behind his back.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Lancashire told him the rationale and then when the members meeting was held, I think Farbrace was abroad, but he dialled in and didn't hide behind the decision.

"He took full accountability for it, so I don't think you can say it's been handled badly."

Anderson made his Lancashire debut in List A cricket in 2001 before a maiden first-class appearance followed a year later.

#1012. Leicester fans furious as club sponsor announces partnership with ‘international porn star’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Foxes Trust said the majority of fans feel negatively about their partnership with BC Game, who announced adult content creator Eva Elfie as an ‘ambassador’ this week

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A Leicester City supporters’ group has urged fans to boycott the club’s home shirt after their sponsor, BC Game, announced a partnership with an “international porn star”.

BC Game, an online casino company who have been Leicester’s front-of-shirt sponsor for the past two years, unveiled Russian adult content creator Eva Elfie as an “ambassador” this week.

A suggestive video featuring Eva Elfie and a man arriving at her door delivering pizza accompanied BC Game’s announcement with the content creator, who also does live streams of video games. “Let the fun begin,” the announcement added.

The Foxes Trust said there has been “dismay and discontent” with BC Game since their sponsorship began and questioned why the club continues to be partners with a company that lost its UK operating licence almost two years ago .

The group said: “Most Leicester City supporters will know by now the Trust’s dismay and discontent with BC Game being our front-of-shirt sponsor. BC Game have now announced a new partnership with ‘international content creator and Esports personality’ Eva Elfie… who just happens to be an international porn star.

“From the moment the club decided to take sponsorship from a betting company we felt Leicester City were ditching its values. Our first article in July 2024 said that ‘It doesn’t feel like who LCFC are to have a gambling website on our shirts and seems to be another step away from our ‘well-run family club’ reputation’.

“The club has not only partnered with a gambling company, but chosen one that is unlicensed to operate in the UK, has unanswered questions about the legitimacy of its funding and its origins, and allows clients to ‘game’ using cryptocurrencies.

“Now throw into the mix that BC Game have entered into a partnership with someone who continues to make their name via adult content. Both gambling and pornography can have devastating impacts on people's lives, in particular young people.

“Partnerships like these bring these two worlds to a larger audience and, by association, link them to Leicester City. Is this who we are now? As always our message is, if you’re purchasing an LCFC replica shirt, opt for one that doesn’t have the BC Game logo on it.”

The former Premier League champions, who now play in League One after consecutive relegations, said they were aware of the BC’s partnership with Eva Elfie and had “raised concerns” with the sponsor.

A club statement said: “Leicester City Football Club recognises the concerns raised about recent developments involving our Principal Partner, BC Game. We have raised these concerns directly with BC Game and are continuing discussions with the company to explore a mutually acceptable resolution.”

The Foxes Trust said an end-of-season survey held in May showed 73 per cent of fans felt “negative” about Leicester’s association with BC Game, with just five per cent of feelings with “content”.

BC Game CEO Ali Muhanned said in a statement: “Eva has built an incredible relationship with the gaming and esports community through genuine passion and consistent content creation. We can’t wait to see what Eva brings to the BC Game community.”

The Reds lost their way after the teenager’s withdrawal in Sunday’s defeat to Arsenal as the midfielder shone on his first ever Premier League start

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola grabbed Trey Nyoni and threw him in at the deep end. Sink or swim was the aim of the game. And the teenager kept his head above water, and then some.

The teenager made his first ever Premier League start on Sunday afternoon. The call was well deserved following a fine showing against Chelsea in the EFL Cup.

That it came against defending champions Arsenal was a huge show of faith in the midfielder. The Reds may have fallen to a narrow 1-0 home defeat to the Gunners, but Nyoni’s 59-minute display proved he’s ready for regular minutes in this Liverpool side.

You’d be forgiven for overlooking Nyoni’s showing at Anfield. Declan Rice, after all, was the star performer on Merseyside. Mikel Arteta’s ‘Master-of-all-Trades’ midfield man put in a dominant display in the middle of the park.

The assist for Kai Havertz’s one and only goal was the cherry on the icing atop the Arsenal cake.

Yet despite coming up against, arguably, one of the best midfielders in world football, Nyoni wasn’t overawed. Rather, he rose to the occasion to deliver a performance that perhaps convinced Iraola he is worthy of a starting spot at the expense of either Alexis Mac Allister or Ryan Gravenberch.

“I just tried to go out there and do what I do, tried to get on the ball as much as possible and bring the team forwards,” Nyoni told the official Liverpool website about making his debut in such a blockbuster event. Many would have been overwhelmed by the spotlight that came from such a moment. Nyoni, though, was buoyed on by the welcome of Arsenal.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The 19-year-old ended the game with the best pass success rate (96.4%) of all starters in Sunday’s match. Only teammates Virgil van Dijk (67) and Mac Allister (61) made more passes than the academy product (56). The former pair played the full 90, whereas the latter was withdrawn on the hour mark.

Nyoni was dictating the tempo in the middle of the park, and driving Liverpool forward. Only Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya (46) made more forward passes than the youngster (24) at the weekend. Fourteen line-breaking passes was the most during his time on the pitch.

Iraola’s decision to withdraw Nyoni in place of the returning Dominik Szoboszlai meant that, for a 15-minute spell, Liverpool ceded momentum as they struggled to gain a foothold on the game.

From the 76th-minute onwards, they again dominated possession, even if it amounted to nothing, but Nyoni’s substitution saw the tie swing back in Arsenal’s favour at a crucial time in the clash. It’s within this 15-minute window where Arteta’s men begin to turn the screw in games. Only Manchester United (33) have had more shots than Arsenal (26) between minutes 60 and 75. Twenty-four chances created ranks top.

Liverpool needed a player who was comfortable in possession to ensure Arsenal were unable to build upon Havertz’s early strike. Of course, the momentum swing didn’t amount to another Gunners goal. Conversely, Liverpool would have enjoyed a more comfortable period of play had Nyoni remained on the pitch.

He brings some much-needed composure in a key area, a quality that had been found wanting following the departure of Curtis Jones. The sidelined Ryan Gravenberch brings the drive from deep, while Mac Allister offers the nitty-gritty, off the ball work to help protect the defence. Nyoni, meanwhile, delivers the forward thrust with his vision and distribution, qualities that far exceed both Gravenberch and Mac Allister, particularly in a 4-2-3-1 setup.

And having been dispossessed just four times in all competitions this season, Nyoni’s press resistance is another important trait. He’s comfortable receiving the ball from the centre-backs, before turning and setting his side on the frontfoot. Even under pressure, you’d back the up-and-coming Reds star to wriggle his way out of danger.

At his age, Nyoni, physically, still has some growing to do. Iraola can be expected to manage his minutes accordingly in order to avoid injury stunting his growth. Regardless, it’s clear that Nyoni is ready for a more prominent role in this Liverpool side.

Former boss Arne Slot used Nyoni sparingly, despite speaking highly of the player. In a difficult second, and final, season in the Anfield dugout, the Dutchman opted for experience. Injuries have perhaps forced Iraola’s hand this time around, but Nyoni has grabbed the opportunity to consolidate a starting spot with both hands.

#1010. Manchester City, the UAE and the UK's PM in a political tangle

Nearly 20 years after arriving in England, Manchester City's UAE owners could exit amid cheating charges. That would pose a challenge for a city — and prime minister — closely tied to Abu Dhabi.

Defiance was the word that stood out as Manchester City returned home for the first time since they were found guilty of 114 financial charges by the Premier League in a case that's made headlines around the world.

City showed a measure of it on the pitch, even as they lost 4-2 to holders, Qatari-owned Paris Saint-Germain, in the Champions League group stages on Wednesday.

Among the home fanbase at the Etihad Stadium, DW found universal support for City's Abu Dhabi owners — headed by Sheikh Mansour, who is also UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister.

"I'm all in with the ownership now," said local fan Matt. "If we end up back in League Two [fourth tier], so be it. We've got 15 years of memories we wouldn't have otherwise and to me it's just an accounting line on a spreadsheet really."

The stadium name itself is a reminder of the takeover that changed this club, and its part of Manchester, in 2008. The national airline of the UAE, Etihad's inflated sponsorship of City is among the key planks of the case against them, while many buildings and businesses around the stadium bear the brand. It's a stadium that's also seen plenty of success of late.

"We've seen things other fans will never see," added fellow City fan Josh. "I think people have got to consider how many people this club has given great memories to, how many people's lives have been changed by it, myself included....you've got to be grateful for that."

Though many in sky blue shared those sentiments, most outside the club now view the trophies won in the relevant period as tarnished. On top of that, critics point to City's reticence in providing evidence in their case, the long-documented human rights abuses in UAE and the often dismissive tone with which the owners have dealt with being found guilty of charges they have now appealed.

But those City fans appear to have one powerful ally in British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Though he has since sought to tone down his position on Mansour and co. somewhat, the former mayor of Greater Manchester said he "would be really concerned to lose them," after the verdict was announced in late September. "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester," he added.

While Burnham has since denied being close to City's ownership, even as City were playing on Wednesday, The Guardian reported a club representative was invited on a government-backed trade delegation to India this week by Burnham's successor as Manchester mayor, Bev Craig.

Earlier the same day, Burnham was forced to confirm he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality. It has become a serious domestic issue for the man who replaced Keir Starmer in July.

What is clear is that Burnham welcomed Abu Dhabi investment during his time in charge of the northwestern city. This came mainly in the form of residential and commercial buildings as well as libraries and sports centers, all popping up in previously run-down areas in and around the stadium.

Georgina Blakeley, a Professor at the University of Huddersfield who wrote a book called "The regeneration of east Manchester," told DW that UAE investment has transformed swathes of the city.

"One of the prime drivers for building this partnership with the Abu Dhabi United Group [a private equity arm of the state mostly concerned with the football club] was that at that point in time, 2014, there was no other private investor willing to invest at the scale that the council wanted. And to do so in a way that created a build-to-rent market," she said.

The UAE investment in Manchester, accelerated by the Manchester Life Partnership with the city's council signed in 2014, has been a key defense for the City owners and fans when faced with sportswashing allegations in the past. And while Blakeley believes councils in the UK are often forced to seek foreign investment, there has been some pushback on how east Manchester has changed.

"A lot of people would be critical of some of the developments in [the districts of] Ancoats and New Islington and say that it's gentrified the area and there are some tensions between newer populations coming in and living in the more expensive flats and those already there. I think there's some truth to it. But I also think there's some truth to the fact that people forget really, really quickly that if you go back to just the 1990s, Ancoats was a no-go area," she said.

While profit for both council and state have certainly been a driver of the partnership, Blakeley thinks that forging greater links to the community could be something City's owners see "as a beneficial side effect."

After 18 years in the club and city, the UAE are deeply embedded in this part of Manchester. With political ties between the UK and UAE now reportedly strained as a result of the charges, there are suggestions that City's owners will try to sell the club. They may also be forced to do so, with sanctions still to be decided pending City's appeal.

There is no such trouble at PSG, who look capable of winning a third straight Champions League powered by their own Gulf-State coffers.

What is clear is that state-owned football clubs can become successful fast in a free market, as the Premier League was when the UAE owners arrived. Deep pockets, strong contacts at the top tables of the sport and canny strategies to integrate with the local area can be a heady mix.

It's certainly one that's proved intoxicating to City's fans, who brush off secret second contracts, sham sponsorship and unreliable witnesses with a loyalty built on success, community and investment. Judging by the mood in Manchester on Wednesday, no sanctions are going to change that.

#1008. Thomas Tuchel explains Cole Palmer omission: ‘He misses too many opportunities’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The England manager has opted to ‘trust’ the players who impressed him in the last squad, while also offering first-time call-ups to Josh King and Jobe Bellingham

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thomas Tuchel says he has “enough” No 10s in his England squad without selecting Cole Palmer, who has paid the price for pulling out of the September camp last time out and missing “too many opportunities to impress”.

The Chelsea star was a notable omission from Tuchel’s 25-man squad ahead of the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain and he was available for selection. Tuchel criticised Palmer for missing “too many camps with injuries” following his withdrawal from last month’s group and the manager has opted to stick with many of the same players who impressed him last time.

Tuchel has named several No 10s in his group, Morgan Rogers, Morgan Gibbs-White, Eberechi Eze, Jude Bellingham, as well as first-time call-ups Josh King and Jobe Bellingham, who both offer versatility in his midfield.

Palmer has not played for England since March and was missed the World Cup after struggling with injuries last season. He has played in all nine of Chelsea’s Premier League matches this season, but was also sent off in the defeat to Tottenham.

Speaking at a press conference at Wembley, Tuchel explained: “It counts when you are in camp and I just said it last time, he misses too many opportunities to impress. It was a long camp. It was two-and-a-half weeks and the players and the boys who were in camp built something extraordinary throughout these weeks.

“That's why the credit goes to them. The trust is for them. If you are in camp, this is your chance to impress. So it's not personal. We will never assume that Cole is not in the mindset to come and desperate to play for his country, but the competition is on and the players who were in camp did an amazing job and kept their place.”

Tuchel added: “There are enough of No 10s, and we stick to the guys who were in camp because camp was excellent and we were happy with the last two-and-half weeks that we had together.

”The impact of all the players was immense throughout the whole camp and that's why we stick mainly with the group. We stick with all the offensive players and we have Josh King as a new player in there, but he can play four positions.”

Palmer was among five players to withdraw from Tuchel’s first England squad since the World Cup, along with Declan Rice, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Tino Livramento. Only vice-captain Rice, who featured heavily at the World Cup, has since been recalled.

Tuchel is not expecting as many withdrawals this time and said he will continue to reward the players who turn up for England and take their opportunities to shine, while adding that he believes his message is getting through to his players.

“It's always about the ones who are in camp,” he said. “It's always the ones who don't withdraw and who walk the talk and come to camp and show that it matters and put the quality in. This is always what we will reward.

“That was always the message very, very early since we took charge, that it matters if you are in camp and it matters what you do in camp. And the last camp was an excellent one.”

#1007. Hearts bruised by Thun in self-inflicted Conference League defeat

FC Thun vs Hearts. UEFA Conference League.

Report as Hearts lose 3-1 to Thun in the Conference League; Jamie McCart's own goal was the first of the errors; Stephen Kingsley gifted another; Stuart Findlay scored a late consolation; the Jambos have one point from their opening three games

Depleted Hearts' Conference League bruising was almost totally self-inflicted in a 3-1 defeat by Thun in Switzerland.

Belgian boss Wouter Vrancken was without 10 players through various ailments and the Scottish team were dealt another blow in the 22nd minute when defender Jamie McCart put through his own goal in calamitous fashion.

Thun doubled their lead in the 33rd minute through striker Brighton Labeau after more poor defending, this time from skipper Stephen Kingsley - who went off later with an injury - and then Furkan Dursun grabbed a third in the 56th minute before Jambos defender Stuart Findlay reduced the deficit in the 82nd minute with a header.

Hearts are left with one Conference League point out of nine following a 1-1 home draw against Nordsjaelland and a 2-0 defeat away to Trabzonspor.

Thick smoke from a pyro halted the game soon after kick-off but when play resumed after a lengthy delay - there were nine minutes added on at the end of the first half - Hearts winger Josh McPake drew a save from Niklas Steffen with an angled drive that lacked real power.

In the 20th minute McPake's effort from 25 yards after he had drifted in from the left had the power but was beaten away by the Thun 'keeper.

There appeared to be nothing untoward on the horizon but then came a Hearts horror show.

There was no real pressure on the Jambos goal when a long ball came into the box but with Lucien Dahler at his shoulder, a simple pass back from McCart somehow evaded Hearts 'keeper Beau Reus and slipped into the corner of the net.

Thun's second goal was also gift-wrapped.

The home side broke clear and with pace following a Heart set-piece and when Nils Reichmuth crossed into the box from the right, Kingsley stuck out a leg to clear but the ball went straight to Labeau who swept it into the net from 10 yards out.

Dursun was shown a yellow card for a forearm challenge into the face of Findlay, and it perhaps deserved more punishment.

The interval gave the Tynecastle side time to reset but, three minutes after the break, Reus made a diving save from Dursun and an even better one from Reichmuth moments later.

However, the 'keeper was beaten once again when Dursun got his toe to a Reichmuth cross.

On the hour mark, Nico Maier raced clear of the Hearts defence but although his chip beat Reus, it sped wide of the target.

The night got worse for the rattled visitors as injured Kingsley was replaced by 19-year-old Matthew Gillies, called back from a loan spell at Stenhousemuir.

Malachi Fagan-Walcott's header from a Jordi Altena free-kick was brilliantly saved by Steffen.

In the 78th minute Jan Bamert had the ball in the net after Steffen tipped a free-kick from substitute Nassim Zoukit on to the bar but was ruled offside, before Findlay headed in a consolation from another Altena free-kick.

"We have to stick together now. We know which situation we're in with all the circumstances.

"And there's only one thing that you have to do now and that is stick together and keep working hard.

"In general, it was not good enough in quality and can you blame them?

"Yeah, on one hand you can because you want to always expect the best and want the best.

"On the other hand, I'm still proud of what they did already in the run-up games."

You have to keep in mind just how exotic foreign players were in the Premier League in 1996, when most sides were made up of British and Irish players, maybe with the odd Scandinavian here or there.

So it's not hard to see why Middlesbrough captured the imagination not just of their own fans, but neutrals too thanks to the signings of Italian superstar Fabrizio Ravanelli and Brazilians Juninho, Emerson and Branco.

And Boro's Australian goalkeeper at the time, Mark Schwarzer, admits that created a bit of a culture shock for all concerned.

Schwarzer told FourFourTwo: "I only played with Fabrizio Ravanelli for my first season there, but I never had any issues with him.

"He just had a level of demand and expectation of players, a level of professionalism that exceeded the norm in England at that time.

"That caused problems with some of the squad. There was also a communication issue with language.

"But it was two different footballing worlds and British players were still adapting.

"You look at what Arsene Wenger brought into Arsenal around diet, well-being and professionalism – that was still in its beginnings in England."

Unfortunately, 'professionalism' was not particularly a watchword for Emerson, who went missing from the squad on multiple occasions as the club increasingly struggled against the threat of relegation.

In Emerson's defence, his wife was reportedly to be desperately unhappy on Teesside - but after finally being sold to Atletico Madrid after another disappearing act following the club's relegation, the midfielder admitted the error of his ways.

Schwarzer said: "I don’t think anybody was surprised. Emo was a phenomenal player, but mad. You just couldn’t control him.

"Even though he went AWOL, everyone still loved him. It was one of those where you should be irate, but you couldn’t because he was such a good guy.

"You just wished that he’d been there for the team more often."

#1005. Why Chinese tech brands are outpacing Western rivals from EVs to robot vacuums

Do you remember the days when GoPro was synonymous with action cameras?

At its peak in 2015, the US company reigned supreme with around 6.6 million units sold that year and a market share of over 70%. Today, the pioneer is fighting for survival.

GoPro's biggest rivals, DJI and Insta360, entered the action camera market in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Today, they account for more than 90% of global smart handheld camera sales.

Alexander Hannemann, who regularly uses action cameras to film his motorcycle rides, says he switched from GoPro to Insta360 around two years ago.

"The quality is much better than a GoPro, even when I'm speeding up and going into corners at like 80 kilometers per hour," he told DW.

GoPro's case is not an exception. Since around 2010, many Chinese brands have not only caught up but surpassed once-dominant Western rivals across the consumer technology industry, from smart TVs to robot vacuums.

Gone are the days when "Made in China" stood for cheap, mass-produced products.

"China is still making affordable products today," says Chris Pereira, a Canadian entrepreneur and author with over 20 years of experience in China. "But the products are also high quality."

This combination has led to well over half of new consumer tech products globally coming from Chinese suppliers, Pereira adds.

BYD, Xpeng and other Chinese car manufactures sold almost two-thirds of all electric cars last year, surpassing incumbents like Tesla. In robot vacuums, Chinese brands dominate the global market, leaving former pioneer US company iRobot struggling to compete.

So why do Chinese companies increasingly outperform their Western rivals?

Pereira, whose consultancy iMpact helps Chinese companies gain traction overseas, attributes China's success to fierce domestic competition in cities like Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Shanghai; highly integrated supply chains and a can-do business culture that allows companies to innovate; and respond to problems quickly.

Other key reasons for China's competitive edge include unparalleled industrial automation, the strategic use of AI in manufacturing, responsiveness from regulators as well as relatively cheap labor, which together leads to significantly lower production costs and much faster innovation cycles than in the world's most advanced economies.

Joey Cheng, who moved to the US for his PhD studies over 20 years ago, is familiar with both the American consumer and the Chinese producer sides.

While his startup is based in the US, almost all the manufacturing is done in Shenzhen, where a large share of the world's hardware and consumer electronics are made.

"The supply chain in Shenzhen is basically inevitable for cost cutting and quick product development," Cheng says. "Especially as a startup you must get the product out quickly, or you'll get blown out of the water."

Although consumers are flocking to Chinese companies, some reservations persist.

A recent poll found that more than 90% of Europeans do not trust Chinese technology companies with their data, while about 80% distrust US firms. Germans expressed the highest level of mistrust.

Nadine, a German travel blogger who uses DJI and Insta360 products, says she wouldn't use any Asian products at home.

"My home robot vacuum is from a German company for precisely this reason: So the data remains compliant with German regulations. After all, manufacturers can connect directly to the camera," she said, referring to camera and audio hacking incidents involving robot vacuums.

Still, Pereira says that Chinese companies expanding abroad have to pay a "trust premium."

"This trust deficit means that they need to be extra competitive in terms of product and price in order for the market to choose them," he says, adding that the gap can be narrowed by a presence in overseas markets like BYD's first European passenger-car plant, expected to open in Hungary later this year.

Chinese companies say they comply with EU data protection rules. However, domestic security laws in the US and China can require firms to hand over data to authorities, and German officials note limited oversight of whether data is transferred from European servers abroad.

In light of security concerns, trade deficits and China's overall dominance, the US and several other Western countries have hit Chinese imports and companies with tariffs, blacklists and strict requirements. In late July, the Trump administration banned the import of humanoid robots manufactured outside the US.

A representative of Chinese robot maker Primebot told DW that all Chinese consumer tech companies are feeling the effects.

"We might seek cooperation with a local US company. Another potential solution is building a factory there," he said.

European countries and the EU are also weighing more tariffs against Chinese companies.

Chris Pereira foresees that the tariffs will accelerate two trends among Chinese companies: Moving more manufacturing overseas and an increasing focus on challenging top-tier Western brands with premium goods.

"Chinese officials and companies recognize that manufacturing needs to be localized to a certain degree. One reason is to assuage the challenges of exporting, another is to create trust locally," Pereira sums up.

"The other trend is that once duties wipe out the price advantage at the bottom, the margin left is at the top, so Chinese brands are increasingly competing directly with established Western names, where trust matters most."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As China's dominance keeps growing, Western companies are scrambling to find ways to stay competitive.

Kaz Merchant, who works for a UK-based company that imports and exports IT hardware, says smaller companies, in particular, must carve out a geographic niche.

"They need to have their own unique selling point for a certain product, which China might not have for that region. Or they need to partner with a Chinese company," he says.

To Pereira, a key issue Europe needs to solve is regulators' responsiveness.

"Chinese regulators tell you very clearly and quickly what you can do. That speed helps companies iterate and succeed overseas," Pereira says.

"If you're waiting weeks for a response, you're going to lose business."

#1004. Inside the indecision at Man United and the question that will decide Michael Carrick’s future

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

A vintage Old Trafford comeback, encouraging underlying numbers and doubts over the list of potential replacements mean there is a growing sense that Carrick could yet survive the international break, writes Miguel Delaney, even if they lose to Aston Villa on Sunday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

As Manchester United returned to the training ground after this week’s Champions League heroics, some there couldn’t help but repeat an old football truth: “Everything feels completely different after a win.”

That will be even more pronounced now, given that United have just ended their longest winless run in 40 years. The 3-2 win over Roma was their first victory since the 4-0 over Sabah, 10 games ago.

Amid the raucous celebrations from a vintage comeback, there was of course considerable relief. It at least, for now, puts off a huge call.

United have been racked by indecision over the future of Michael Carrick. Numerous sources say there is a sense that no one was actually willing to make a call on the manager, a problem compounded by the fact they have “little idea” over a replacement.

In fairness, there are questions and debates over all of the main alternatives.

United are understood to be much less sold on Eddie Howe than perception would have it. Sebastian Hoeness is highly rated, but his appointment would still involve a huge Ruben Amorim-like leap from Stuttgart. Fabian Hurzeler might struggle without Brighton’s structure amid higher stakes, and there are doubts over whether United can even afford the compensation. Cesc Fabregas is impressing at Como but isn’t going anywhere for now, and is viewed as Mikel Arteta’s eventual successor at Arsenal.

Julian Nagelsmann’s stock has significantly dropped, meanwhile. While United’s Christoph Vivell is said to be a fan, others in the hierarchy will be aware that Bayern Munich would not speak highly about his time there. The players didn’t respond well to his approach or personality, and the image persists of Nagelsmann arriving to training on a skateboard. It is hard not to think of a line from The Sopranos. In the same way “a don doesn’t wear shorts”, a Manchester United manager doesn’t have a skateboard.

You can’t imagine that of Antonio Conte, a title winner at four different clubs who is one of the very few to have done it at the required level. The question is whether United’s squad is of the level to ensure they would at least get the good season you usually do out of the Italian, before an inevitable blow-up.

If all of this sounds harsh on Carrick given he’s just won again, it’s of course about the reality that all of the same concerns could rush back after the next game.

And that next game is against Aston Villa’s Unai Emery, who looks set to stay Aston Villa's Unai Emery. As has been said on these pages many times, football has that extraordinary capacity to throw up a narratively fitting fixture at a moment when a story is huge.

So, on the 40th anniversary of Sir Alex Ferguson’s appointment, United welcome a coach who some in the hierarchy do see as a potential figurehead for the modern age.

And, up until Tuesday, this last game before the international break had been cast as an inevitable curtain closer – at least for Carrick.

A burgeoning Villa side were surely just going to expose and exploit United’s myriad problems, just before a lot of time to think.

Except, United finally got that win, just as Emery’s team endure a bump ahead of a trip to a stadium where they have a dismal record. Villa have only won one game at Old Trafford in 15 years, and Emery has never won there at all.

If this all sounds an overt focus on psychology and form, the truth is it especially matters to United right now.

One of a few reasons they haven’t yet made a call on Carrick – to go with indecision – is because of the underlying numbers.

The data shows that United haven’t been quite as bad as they’ve appeared, even if it still hasn’t been great. The numbers have been almost identical to last season.

One belief is that the team, this time, have found themselves on the wrong side of the margins, which are very thin, in a complete reversal of last season. A few key moments have gone against them, which has further affected confidence at a fragile moment.

The whole performance against Chelsea summed this up. United were good in the first half, only to fail to take some big chances, and then buckled as Lisandro Martinez was sent off.

That has come amid a sense they didn’t back Carrick to the extent they should have in the summer, which is why they are just trying to get through this period and then do more business in January.

The hope has been that the team just needed that one win, that break, to end this current spiral.

It’s entirely possible that’s what the Roma victory may represent.

United themselves have enough experience of this.

They’ve experienced almost this exact situation before, too. Back in October 2021, just a month before Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was sacked, United came back from 2-0 down in the Champions League to beat a Gian Piero Gasperini Serie A team 3-2. It was then Atalanta rather than Roma, but it was still the same problem: a temporary balm.

And, just like then, it’s entirely possible the Roma win may lull United into a thinking that other clubs constantly say is so damaging to them. That is that they are always just “a few tweaks” from being there, when they still ultimately need that deep overhaul. Even if they beat Villa and go on a better run, does anyone really believe there won’t eventually be a regression?

The Ineos leadership have admittedly attempted to start that process, but it’s so far only been an attempt. They’re trying. They’re not yet succeeding.

As one chief executive who has direct experience of this process says, “it’s not actually difficult to figure out, but it’s hard to execute. What is absolutely crucial is to get quality people in the right positions.”

Again, a vision around which everything works and the nerve to commit to it. Do United have any of that?

Another issue right now is that the entire place is said to be enduring extreme emotional swings. The performances are of course the main factor, but so is the media industrial complex around the club. There's this constant noise.

Sir Jim Ratcliffe is so conscious of what Gary Neville’s United empire says, for example, that he did an interview with him.

The events of the last week show Villa can be given to emotional swings themselves, but the action over Emery’s future – and anticipated new contract – also shows a decisiveness that has been missing at United.

For United’s part, it is riskier for them, given their scale, to do what Villa did with Emery and give a manager the keys to the club.

That is also a model they’ve long wanted to move away from. They really don’t need to get into yet another cycle that just goes around and around.

For now, an uncertainty remains, right up to what next for the team.

#1003. Gloucestershire set to change name to Bristol for T20 Blast

Name change will apply to men's and women's teams for T20 cricket; Warwickshire competed as Birmingham Bears from 2014 to 2025 before reverting to traditional county name; Gloucestershire have won the men's Blast once, back in 2024 when they beat Somerset in the final

Gloucestershire are set to drop their county name in the T20 Blast and rebrand to Bristol from 2027 onwards.

The club confirmed in a statement that they will be creating a new T20 identity for their men's and women's teams and have made the decision "as part of our wider strategic vision to grow domestic cricket, attract new audiences across the region, and drive commercial reinvestment back into the sport."

The club will continue to operate as Gloucestershire in the County Championship and One Day Cup.

A club statement issued on Friday said: "Over recent months, Gloucestershire County Cricket Club has worked closely with our players, our Members Working Group, the ECB, and a number of key stakeholders to help shape an exciting new chapter in our evolution.

"Building on more than 150 years of proud heritage, Gloucestershire Cricket will always remain our overarching identity and the foundation of everything we do.

"As part of our wider strategic vision to grow domestic cricket, attract new audiences across the region, and drive commercial reinvestment back into the sport, we will be creating a new dedicated T20 identity for our men's and women's teams.

"Full details of our plans and brand identity moving forward will soon be officially unveiled, in alignment with the forthcoming ECB national domestic fixture release.

"We look forward to sharing our complete vision with our fans, partners and media in the near future."

Warwickshire played under the Birmingham Bears moniker in the Blast from 2014, before reverting to their traditional county name ahead of the 2026 campaign.

Gloucestershire have won the men's Blast once in their history, in 2024 when they defeated Somerset in the final.

The county were also runners-up to Kent back in 2007.

Northamptonshire Steelbacks won the men's Blast in 2026, with The Blaze claiming the women's title.

Arsenal star Mikel Merino has been linked with a return to his homeland

The father of Arsenal star Mikel Merino has explained the conditions in which his son will depart the club.

Merino has established himself as a cult hero at Arsenal, playing as a makeshift centre-forward during injury crises and chipping in with vital goals, but since moving to North London in the summer of 2024, he hasn't established himself as a first choice in manager Mikel Arteta's midfield.

This has led to talk that he could depart the Emirates Stadium for a return to Spain, as he looks to play more regularly for club and country.

As relayed by Sport Witness, Spain manager Luis de la Fuente has relegated Merino to a substitute role with the national team, while the midfielder played just 193 minutes at the World Cup.

Last month, Merino's father – Angel Miguel, a former professional footballer himself – laid out the conditions for his son moving back to La Liga, claiming, “he’ll want to continue in that rhythm of competing in the Champions League and keeping that motivation”.

Spanish outlet La Razon has since reported that Atletico Madrid want to sign the La Roja star on loan with a purchase option.

The 30-year-old has started just once in the Premier League this term but started three of Arsenal's four Champions League games, with Arteta using him as an alternative No.10 option to Martin Odegaard.

With Arsenal boasting the likes of Declan Rice, Martin Zubimendi, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes in midfield, Merino's chances of starting regularly are slim, but Arteta has leaned on his hold-up play and close control to help see out matches this season, with the star appearing in every single fixture so far.

FourFourTwo understands that Arsenal value Merino as a key member of the squad, however, despite the limited minutes.

The Spaniard is one of Arteta's leadership group, taking the captaincy from Odegaard on occasion in the Norwegian's absence this season, with many suggesting that Merino will take up coaching in the future.

Merino's contract runs until 2028, but with Arsenal in no desperate need to raise funds or sell a player in his prime, they could still choose to hold on to the midfielder until the end of his deal.

No discussions have taken place about an extension for the midfielder.

Merino is worth €25 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal host Hull City this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

#1001. ‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. Paediatrician Annie Andrews, a Democrat, won a US Senate seat in South Carolina in a surprise victory on 3 November. Democrats had not won a Senate seat in the state since 1998.Credit: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty

The US mid-term elections swept the Democratic party to power in both chambers of the US Congress, raising hopes that lawmakers will now push back against disruptions to science introduced by the administration of Republican President Donald Trump.

The results will mark the end of nearly two years in which the Republicans controlled the presidency and both congressional chambers — and many scientists around the world are celebrating the change as an opportunity to protect the country’s research system.

How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

“This is a big win,” says Megan Peters, a cognitive scientist who moved in 2025 from the University of California, Irvine, to University College London in part because of worries about US science. “It’s a demonstration that US [voters] are dissatisfied with what the current administration has been doing.” Scientific research, she adds, “is America’s superpower, and it’s been cut at the knees”.

Those hopeful for change include researchers affected by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) being shut down early in Trump’s presidency. “I’m cautiously optimistic,” says Quarraisha Abdool Karim, an epidemiologist at the Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa, which is headquartered in Durban and had partnered with USAID on clinical trials. “What we’ve seen in the past 24 hours is that democracy and democratic principles, with individuals turning out to vote, can make a huge difference.” But, she adds, “we will not see overnight changes”.

As of 2.15 p.m. EST on 4 November, Democrats had secured at least 237 seats in the 435-seat US House of Representatives and 54 seats in the 100-member US Senate, giving them decisive majorities in both, with votes still being counted in some states. These majorities will give them the power to craft legislation that counteracts Trump’s science agenda, although there will still be obstacles. For instance, given that Democrats haven’t won two-thirds of the seats in both chambers of Congress, the president can veto those bills.

Trump initially told The New York Times that he would accept the mid-term election results and that he would “look forward” to working with Democrats. Later, however, he posted an image of a red hat with the word ‘VETO’ on it to Truth Social, his social-media platform.

Since Donald Trump became president for the second time in January 2025, his administration has pushed for unprecedented cuts to science funding, politicized decision-making at federal science agencies and interfered with policies at US universities that receive federal funding.

When Democrats take charge of both chambers of the US Congress on 3 January 2027, they will be able to control congressional committees, including science committees; set agendas for hearings that investigate government officials and their science policies; and use legally binding subpoenas to compel the Trump administration to provide documents and testify in front of Congress.

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

On social media, Democrats promised to make use of that authority. Robert Garcia, a representative from California who will soon chair the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, shared a two-word statement aimed at the Trump administration: “Lawyer up.” In particular, some scientists are calling for scrutiny of Russell Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, who has drafted a plan that gives political appointees, rather than scientist peer reviewers, control of decisions about research grants, and who has delayed the distribution of congressionally-approved science funds.

Scientists and policy specialists said they were hoping to see more congressional oversight of the actions of Robert F. Kennedy Jr, the head of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) who has questioned vaccine safety and whose tenure has coincided with the country’s worst measles resurgence in decades. “For sure, Secretary Kennedy will be put on the hot seat” to explain his unscientific actions, says Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association in Washington DC. “What I’m hoping is that Congress will really push this administration to have a much more proactive response to the measles epidemic.”

Zoe Lofgren, a Democratic representative from California, said she would campaign to become the head of the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, which oversees agencies such as NASA and the US National Science Foundation. “We will hold this administration accountable for the damage they have done to the American scientific enterprise,” she said in a statement.

Stand Up for Science (SUFS), a science-advocacy group based in Atlanta, Georgia, that has organized protests against the Trump administration’s reshaping of US science, says that it will release a plan on 5 November with strategies to push Congress for change.

Whether Congress will be able to increase funding for federal science, rather than just hold it relatively steady as they have for the past two years, is doubtful, however. Susan Collins, a Republican senator from Maine and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, had protected science budgets but she lost her re-election bid in these mid-terms. Large boosts to science spending could also just be difficult to pass, given that the budget must also be signed by Trump, who has tried to slash non-defence science spending.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03579-x

With additional reporting from Kaia Glickman, Mariana Lenharo and Anne Pichon.

#1000. Thomas Tuchel hands Jobe Bellingham the chance to carve his own path as an England star

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

From childhood Champions League finals on a patch of grass in Stourbridge to the biggest stage in international football, Jobe Bellingham is determined to step out of his brother’s shadow

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Jobe Bellingham’s football career is strikingly similar to that of his big brother Jude, from the unusual Birmingham-to-Dortmund route right down to their distinctive rangey stride, and so far it has been a case of, anything you can do, I did it faster, better, with a little more panache. But there is one thing Jude didn’t tick off on his meteoric rise – he never captained England Under-21s.

Proudly wearing the armband in September, Jobe shone in a 4-2 comeback win over Kazakhstan in qualifying for next year’s U21 Euros. It was another sign that the 21-year-old’s development is rapidly accelerating.

“He was outstanding,” U21s manager Lee Carsley said. “I went to watch Jobe a couple of weeks ago in Dortmund and he’s progressing so quickly. Physically he’s grown. He’s definitely got that strength in his legs. He’s moving the ball so well and his footwork has really improved. The way he’s moving the ball, taking opponents on, and using his strength and balance … he was always a good player but now he’s going through the levels.”

That, Thomas Tuchel stressed in his Wembley press conference on Friday, was the primary reason for Jobe’s first call-up to the senior England squad, a landmark earned “on his own merit”. The Bellingham brothers are both included in the 25-man group to face Croatia here on Thursday and Spain in Madrid on Sunday, as England – who have virtually qualified for the Nations League quarter-finals in March – go all out to win Group A3.

“Lee is speaking very, very highly of him,” Tuchel explained. “In the Under-21s, he’s a standout player since a long time now. He’s the captain. So I think the door should always be open for that pathway, for special performances over a long period of time, and that’s what Jobe has done.

“He has also found his rhythm with Dortmund, he’s had an excellent start to the season. He’s a regular starter now there and very influential. So there’s an opportunity coming on his own merit. Jobe deserves to make an impression and that’s why we’re glad to have him in camp and see what he can do for us.”

Jobe wears his first name on the back of his shirt, partly in an effort to distinguish himself from his brother, now a fully fledged galactico at Real Madrid who shone at the 2026 World Cup and already has 60 international caps to his name at 23.

“When I signed for Sunderland it was suggested to me by someone, a special coach I had there,” Jobe explained. “I was still young and thought it was cool to have my own name on the back. It didn’t have any deeper meaning but it’s become something unique. It shows that I’m going my own way. Some people don’t like it – I don’t care.”

The comparisons, of course, are inevitable. Both brothers made their debuts for Birmingham City aged 16 before moving to Dortmund – Jude aged 17 in a £25m transfer, Jobe via a successful two-season stint at Sunderland where he won Championship Young Player of the Season, later moving to the German club aged 19 for £28m.

Anyone would think Jobe might choose a different club in order to carve his own path, but he recognised that it would be damaging to make career choices simply to avoid his brother’s footprints, even if he had “fears” before joining Dortmund, where Jude grew into a global star. “It’s not about being different,” Jobe said. “It’s about doing the right thing.”

The brothers are close. They spent every possible minute of their childhood playing football on a small square of grass outside the family home in Stourbridge, up until it got dark. “Every game we played, we always said it was the Champions League final,” said Jude in 2022, two years before winning the actual Champions League final with Real Madrid. “We’d make up teams and make up stadiums that we’d play in. We must have played about 1,000 Champions League finals on that little patch of grass.”

They are both fast, strong and physically imposing central midfielders, standing 6ft plenty, with huge technical ability, coached into them by their father Mark who had a nomadic career as a prolific striker in non-league football. Incidentally, Mark Bellingham has been starring for England recently too, after scoring seven goals on his debut for the England Over-50s Veterans in a 13-1 win against the Republic of Ireland.

But there are also differences in how they play the game. Jude’s strengths are in an advanced No 8 or No 10 role, surging forwards with the ball at his feet, gliding past tacklers, holding off markers and impacting the game with goals. Jobe is more of a traditional box-to-box midfielder with an excellent reading of the game, someone who sits a little deeper and can lay a platform for more attacking teammates.

There is another difference. Jobe is an altogether more low-key figure, and has said he does not wish to “be a superstar... I don’t want to be a big character away from the pitch. When I play I just want to be one of the highest performing players and get my head down.”

Jobe now has the opportunity to begin his own journey as an England international. He will do so not as Jude’s younger brother, but as a midfielder who has earned his chance. Though if he does make his senior debut, Jobe might just happen to have his biggest fan beside him. “As long as he’s happy, that’s all I really care about,” Jude said recently. “His happiness means more to me than my own.”

FourFourTwo's dedicated FPL columnist, and one of the top players in the world, BigManBakar selects his best differentials for GW10

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nine gameweeks in, the managers climbing the ranks are rarely the ones sitting on the same 15 players as everyone else.

Rank gains tend to come from backing someone the crowd has overlooked at the right moment. For this piece, a differential is any player owned by 15% or fewer FPL managers, and there are some strong ones available right now.

These are the six I would be looking at for Gameweek 10.

Thierno Barry (£5.6m, 7.6% owned) vs Coventry (h)

At £5.6m, Barry is some of the best value in the game, and the price alone makes him easy to fit in as an attacker for the weeks ahead. Only Erling Haaland has a higher Expected Goal (xG) involvement this season. People like to say he can't finish, but he scored eight from roughly 8.5 xG last year, which is hardly poor. Penalties could come his way as well, and Coventry at home is about as friendly as fixtures get.

Jarrad Branthwaite (£5.5m, 2.2% owned) vs Coventry (h)

Branthwaite is fit again and anchors an Everton side that has already kept four clean sheets. Coventry rank 20th for xG, and Everton carry some of the best clean sheet odds in the league. He also picks up defensive contributions, which gives him a solid points floor, and he is a differential route into the fixture that very few managers have noticed yet.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Luka Vuskovic (£5.2m, 7.4% owned) vs Brentford (h)

Expect Vuskovic to become hugely popular, especially with managers hunting an Ezri Konsa replacement. He is nailed on to play, good for defensive contributions, carries a goal threat and affordable.

Brighton are joint-top for clean sheets, and their schedule is strong, starting with Brentford at home this week before Hull City and Newcastle United in the weeks to follow.

Dominik Szoboszlai (£6.7m, 13.4% owned) vs Crystal Palace (a)

Szoboszlai is back and fit, which makes him a big differential again. He takes set pieces, might be on penalties and has bonus potential, so he has several ways to score points.

Palace have conceded more goals than any other side this season, and that gives his upside a nice boost for this one.

Matheus Cunha (£7.8m, 5.5% owned) vs Aston Villa (h)

Cunha scored twice in the Champions League against Roma and should be well placed for plenty of minutes against Villa. Man United have struggled in recent weeks, but a comeback like that against Roma could be just what they need to get going again. He is a fresh, lower owned way into a Man United attack that has been out of form but is far from short of ability.

Antonio Silva (£5.1m, 2.6% owned) vs Ipswich (a)

Silva has a good fixture this week and a very strong run directly after it. Bournemouth are in the top three for xG Conceded (xGC), even after a tough opening run in the first eight gameweeks. He is a near-certainty to start, good for defensive contributions and has encouraging underlying numbers for attacking threat, so he has plenty of routes to points.

At 2.6% ownership, he is one of the cheapest ways to get ahead of the field at the back.

Cristiano Ronaldo international curtain call is a bitter affair and sorry stain on one of the greats' legacies

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

To the very end, Cristiano Ronaldo wants ownership of the narrative.

Ahead of Jorge Jesus' Portugal squad announcement for the upcoming November international break, Ronaldo has officially retired from the international side of the game.

Ronaldo's retirement statement was polished and studio-produced, framing his departure from international football as a considered, dignified decision of a man bowing out on his own terms. But nobody in football should be fooled by the PR surrounding his Portugal farewell. Ronaldo is not walking away because of his obligation to 'hand back the No. 7 shirt'; he is jumping before he's pushed.

With Portugal’s squad announcement for the November international window imminent, whispers had grown impossible to ignore, especially after the histrionics which made headlines during the most recent international break.

For everything we know about Ronaldo and the opinion he holds of himself, the prospect of reading a squad list without his name on it would have been unbearable.

No matter how it's dressed up, his exit from the international scene is an undignified end for a footballer of his stature, burning the house down rather than accept that time had finally caught up with him.

The genesis of the split came during the conjoined September and October international camps, where Ronaldo's conduct reflected entitled petulance. He could have chosen to be an experienced mentor to one of Europe's most gifted squads, but instead behaved emotionally, putting self before side.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

When substituted early during Portugal's Nations League fixture against Wales, the 41-year-old trudged off, held his tongue but not for very long.

From the outset, Jesus had made it clear that Portugal’s tactical system would no longer be warped to accommodate Ronaldo. The new coach wants aggressive front-foot pressing, off-the-ball running, and quick transitions, which Ronaldo is simply incompatible with. Tensions reportedly grew in training over Ronaldo’s lack of engagement in defensive drills and his habit of dropping deep into midfield spaces, disrupting the collective shape to hunt for touches.

"After the National Team Coach's press conference, and following a conversation with the President of the Portuguese Football Federation, I made the decision to leave the National Team camp," Ronaldo wrote in a statement after being left out entirely against Norway. "In due time, I will tell the truth to all Portuguese people about the reasons that motivated my departure from the national team, to which I have always dedicated myself. Now is the time to wish good luck to Portugal and to all my teammates, without exception."

The ensuing media storm hijacked Portugal’s camp leaving teammates fielding questions about their captain's bruised ego rather than their own football.

That the curtain falls in this manner is a tragedy for international football. His 146 goals, 234 appearances, alarming longevity and bordering-on-delusional drive made him more than a footballer. Even his detractors will concede, he's earned the right to a fairytale farewell, which no doubt would have been a tearful, adoring lap of honour in Lisbon, where his career began over 20 years ago.

Now, though, he slips out through the side exit, some might say motivated by spite and wanting to save face. There will be no emotional testimonial or triumphant send-off, at least not yet. Cristiano Ronaldo may have spared himself the humiliation of being dropped, but in doing so, has traded in his hero’s goodbye.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League.
